pack: Witnesses outside the Gospels: the death of Jesus

properties.name: Tacitus — Annals 15.44 (Rome)
properties.found: Roman senator-historian Tacitus (c. 116 CE) reports that "Christus" was executed under Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate, in the context of Nero blaming Christians for the fire of 64 CE.
properties.support: Latin, Annals 15.44 (short key words: 'Christus ... supplicio adfectus erat'). Paraphrase: the man the name comes from, Christus, was put to death under Tiberius by Pontius Pilate.
properties.notes: Native language: Latin. Written at Rome. Hostile witness, calls the movement a "superstition".
properties.caveat: Overwhelmingly accepted as authentic; debate is over his source (Roman records vs. Christian hearsay) and the "procurator" title (Pilate was technically prefect).
properties.author: Publius Cornelius Tacitus
caveats: Text is accepted as genuine by nearly all scholars.
Minor debate: where Tacitus got his facts (Roman files or what Christians said).
He calls Pilate 'procurator'; in Jesus' time the title was 'prefect' (Pilate inscription, Caesarea).
A small debate exists over whether the oldest manuscript first read 'Chrestianos'; it does not change the point.

properties.name: Josephus — Antiquities 18.63-64 & 20.200 (Rome)
properties.found: Jewish historian Flavius Josephus (c. 93-94 CE) mentions Jesus, "a wise man", condemned to the cross by Pilate (18.63-64, the Testimonium Flavianum), and James "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ" (20.200).
properties.support: Greek. 20.200 (short): 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, named James.' 18.64 paraphrase: after leading men accused him, Pilate sentenced him to the cross.
properties.notes: Native language: Greek (Josephus was a Judean writing in Rome under Flavian patronage). An Arabic paraphrase preserved by Agapius of Hierapolis (10th c.) gives a more neutral wording.
properties.caveat: Most scholars hold 18.63-64 has a genuine core with later Christian interpolations ("he was the Christ"); 20.200 is widely accepted as authentic.
properties.author: Flavius Josephus
caveats: Most scholars think 18.63-64 has a real core that Christian copyists later added to (lines like 'he was the Christ').
A few scholars think the whole passage was added; a few think all of it is genuine.
20.200 about James is accepted by most scholars.

properties.name: Mara bar Serapion — Letter to his son (Samosata)
properties.found: A Syriac letter (after 73 CE?) by a Stoic prisoner from Samosata asks what the Jews gained by killing their "wise king", alongside Socrates and Pythagoras.
properties.support: Syriac letter, British Library Add. MS 14658. Paraphrase: the Jews gained nothing by executing their wise king, since their kingdom was taken away.
properties.notes: Native language: Syriac. Author location: Samosata (Commagene, now under Atatürk Dam lake, Turkey). Does not name Jesus.
properties.caveat: Date disputed (73 CE to 3rd c.); identification of the "wise king" with Jesus is probable but not certain.

properties.name: Thallus via Julius Africanus (Rome / Emmaus-Nicopolis)
properties.found: Julius Africanus (c. 221 CE), writing at Emmaus-Nicopolis, says Thallus explained the darkness at the crucifixion as a solar eclipse — which Africanus rejects since Passover falls at full moon.
properties.support: Greek fragment preserved in George Syncellus. Paraphrase: Thallus calls this darkness an eclipse of the sun, unreasonably, it seems to me.
properties.notes: Thallus himself wrote in Greek (mid-1st c.? at Rome); his work is lost. Pin is at Emmaus-Nicopolis where Africanus lived.
properties.caveat: Thallus' date and whether he actually mentioned Jesus are disputed; known only third-hand.

properties.name: Phlegon of Tralles — Olympiads (Tralles)
properties.found: Phlegon, freedman of Hadrian, recorded a great eclipse and earthquake in Olympiad 202 (c. 32-33 CE); Origen and Africanus link it to the crucifixion darkness.
properties.support: Greek fragment via Eusebius/Africanus/Origen (Contra Celsum 2.33, 2.59). Paraphrase: in the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad there was a great eclipse, night at the sixth hour, and an earthquake in Bithynia.
properties.notes: Native language: Greek. Author location: Tralles (Aydın, Turkey), working at Rome.
properties.caveat: Phlegon did not mention Jesus himself in surviving fragments; the eclipse link is a Christian inference, and a real solar eclipse of 29 CE (Nov 24) may be meant.
properties.author: Phlegon of Tralles
properties.date_range: Olympiads written c. 137-140s CE; eclipse dated Olympiad 202.4 = 32/33 CE
caveats: Phlegon's surviving words do not mention Jesus; Christian writers made the link.
Known only through later quotes (Africanus, Origen, Eusebius), and the year wording differs between quotes.
A real solar eclipse on 24 Nov 29 CE fits his report better than a Passover darkness.

properties.name: Pliny the Younger — Letter 10.96 (Amastris / Bithynia)
properties.found: Governor Pliny (c. 112 CE) writes to Trajan about Christians who sing hymns "to Christ as to a god" and asks how to try them.

properties.caveat: Authentic; does not mention the crucifixion directly — evidences early worship of Christ.

properties.name: Suetonius — Claudius 25.4 / Nero 16.2 (Rome)

properties.caveat: "Chrestus" is likely a garbled Christus, but could be an unrelated person; says nothing about the death itself.

properties.name: Lucian of Samosata — Death of Peregrinus 11, 13 (Athens)
properties.found: Satirist Lucian (c. 165 CE) mocks Christians who worship "that crucified sophist" executed in Palestine for introducing a new cult.

properties.notes: Native language: Greek. Lucian was from Samosata but wrote Peregrinus while living in Athens.
properties.caveat: Authentic but late and satirical; reflects 2nd-c. public knowledge rather than independent records.

properties.name: Qur'an 4:157 (Medina)
properties.found: The Qur'an (7th c.) addresses the crucifixion, denying that Jesus was killed or crucified — "it was made to appear so to them".
properties.support: Arabic: "وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ" — they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them (shubbiha lahum).
